blocks.text: IELTS LISTENING

Listening is the fairest module in IELTS and the one most students underestimate. It is fair because the answers are all there, spoken clearly, in order. It is underestimated because the recording plays once and will not wait for you. You cannot reread a sentence you missed the way you can in Reading. This single fact changes everything about how you should behave, and this module is built around it.

You will not improve your Listening score by “listening harder.” You will improve it by knowing exactly what to do in the seconds before each part begins, exactly what your ear should be waiting for, exactly how the test tries to trick you, and exactly how to recover when you slip. That is what the next chapters install. We begin where every good strategy begins: understanding how the test is actually built.
PART 1
Understanding IELTS Listening

You cannot outsmart a test you do not understand. Most candidates walk in with a vague picture of the Listening test. A high scorer walks in knowing the shape of every part, the moment each answer will arrive, and the traps waiting inside each one.

Four parts. Forty questions. Ten questions in each part. Roughly thirty minutes of audio. Every recording is played once only, and the answers come in the same order as the recording. The answer to question 3 will always be spoken before the answer to question 4. This ordering is one of your most powerful tools, and we will use it constantly. Difficulty climbs as you move through the parts: Part 1 is the gentlest, Part 4 is the hardest, and you should plan your energy around it.

rows: Talk about a place, event, or facility

blocks.text: Part 1 is an everyday conversation, usually one person giving information (names, dates, prices, addresses) while the other writes it down. Most answers are simple facts, and these are the cheapest marks in the whole exam — aim to get all ten.

Part 2 is a monologue in an everyday context: a talk about a facility, a set of instructions, a description of a place. Because only one person speaks, the speaker's own signposting (first, next, on your left, the main change is) becomes your map.

Part 3 is a conversation between up to four people in an educational context, usually students and a tutor discussing an assignment or piece of research. Difficulty jumps here: multiple voices, opinions that agree and disagree, and decisions that get changed halfway through a sentence. Distractors live here in large numbers.

Part 4 is an academic monologue, a single speaker giving a university-style lecture. Longer stretches of speech, denser information, fewer pauses, and often no chance to catch your breath. Concentration is the whole game in Part 4.
Timing, and a change most books get wrong

For years, IELTS Listening ended with ten extra minutes to copy your answers onto a separate answer sheet, and older books still teach that. This is out of date. IELTS is delivered by computer at nearly all centres now, and on the computer-delivered test there is no ten-minute transfer. You type each answer directly on the screen as you hear it, and at the end you get only about two minutes to review what you have typed.

items: You do not “listen now and write neatly later.” You capture the answer the instant you hear it, in the box, while the audio keeps moving.
Your two-minute review at the end is for catching obvious slips, not for reconstructing answers from memory. Anything left blank now is almost certainly gone.
You can make notes and highlight on screen during the audio, so use that. Jot a rough version fast, then tidy it in the same gap if there is one.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: Practise on a screen, not on paper. The single most common shock on test day for students who prepared on paperbacks is discovering there is no comfortable transfer time and the answer must go straight into the box. Train the way you will play.
blocks.bn: পরীক্ষা এখন কম্পিউটারে হয়, কাগজে নয়। তাই স্ক্রিনে অনুশীলন করুন, উত্তর সঙ্গে সঙ্গে বক্সে লিখুন।

blocks.text: How the information reaches you

Before each part, a voice tells you to look at a set of questions and gives you a short pause to read them. This pause is gold: it is your only chance to prepare, and how you use it separates bands. During the audio, the answers arrive embedded in natural speech, almost never in the same words as the question. The exam is testing whether you can recognise the same meaning wearing different clothes — the deepest principle of the entire module.

Twelve question types recur throughout the test: form, note, table, flow-chart, summary, and sentence completion; multiple choice; multiple-answer; matching; map labelling; diagram labelling; and short-answer questions.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: Do not practise only the types you find easy. Students who drill form completion and multiple choice for weeks are ambushed when a whole section turns out to be map labelling or matching. Every type must feel familiar before test day.
blocks.bn: শুধু সহজ টাইপ অনুশীলন করবেন না। পরীক্ষার আগেই প্রতিটি প্রশ্নের ধরনের সঙ্গে পরিচিত হন।

blocks.text: How distractors work (a first look)

A distractor is information the exam plants to pull you towards the wrong answer. It is not an accident; it is designed. The most common form is the correction: a speaker gives one piece of information, then changes it (“So that will be room 214, sorry, room 240.”). If you write the first number and relax, you lose the mark; the word “sorry” was the signal. Another common form is two plausible options where both are mentioned but only one is chosen (“We could meet on Wednesday, but Thursday actually works better.”). Hearing a word is not the same as that word being the answer — we return to this constantly.
How the raw score becomes a band
Every correct answer is worth one mark, out of forty, with no penalty for wrong answers, so never leave a blank. The raw score converts to the nine-band scale, and the table below is indicative.

Read this table strategically. To reach Band 7 you can afford to miss nine or ten answers. That knowledge should calm you: a single lost answer is not a disaster, and chasing it in panic can cost far more than the one mark it was worth. Protecting the marks you can still get is almost always the better trade.
PART 2
The Listening Mindset
Two students can have the same level of English and score two full bands apart in Listening. The difference is almost never in the ears. It is in the head.

Listening is not a comprehension exercise. It is a live hunt: can you catch specific pieces of information as they fly past, once, while also reading, predicting, and recovering, all at the same time? The information moves in one direction and never comes back.

Reading ahead is your only real weapon. You cannot control the recording; the one thing you fully control is what you do in the pauses before and between parts. Reading ahead means understanding what each upcoming question asks and preparing your ear for what it must catch, so that when the answer arrives, a bell rings. A candidate who has read ahead is waiting for the answer; a candidate who has not is reacting to it, always half a second too late.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: In the pause before each part, do not read every word of every question. Read the gaps and the words immediately around them. You are building a small set of “listen for this” targets, not studying a text.
blocks.bn: অডিও শুরুর আগে বিরতিতে প্রতিটি শব্দ পড়বেন না। শুধু ফাঁকা জায়গা ও তার আশেপাশের শব্দ দেখুন, কী শুনতে হবে তা মাথায় রাখুন।

blocks.text: Once you have read ahead, predict the shape of each gap, not the exact answer. Before the audio you should already suspect: this gap needs a number, this one needs a name, this one needs a plural noun, this one is a time or a date. Prediction turns thirty minutes of overwhelming sound into a series of small, targeted catches.

You need both listening for specific information (a single fact: price, platform number, surname — form, note, and table completion live here) and listening for meaning (the overall sense: attitude, agreement, direction — multiple choice, matching, and much of Parts 3 and 4 live here). The expert candidate knows, from the question type, which mode to be in before the audio starts.

In Parts 2 and 4, follow the speaker's own structure words (firstly, the next thing to note, however, the main reason) as a handrail through the talk. In Part 3, you must also track who is speaking and what each person thinks, since questions often hang on exactly that.

Thirty minutes of continuous listening is genuinely tiring, and attention naturally dips, especially in the long Part 4 monologue. Attention is a budget: spend it on the approach to each answer, not evenly across every second. Relax slightly the instant after you have safely captured an answer, then sharpen again as the next question approaches.

You will miss answers — every high scorer does. What separates them is what they do in the next two seconds. The disaster is not the miss; the disaster is chasing it, because while your mind stays on the lost answer, the recording delivers the next one too. The reflex to build is the clean reset: recognise the miss, let it go instantly, and rejoin the audio at the next question.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: One missed answer should never cost you the next three. The panic costs more marks than the miss. The moment you feel yourself reaching backwards for a lost answer, drop it and move your eyes to the next question.
blocks.bn: একটি উত্তর মিস করলে সেটির পেছনে ছুটবেন না। মিস হলে সঙ্গে সঙ্গে ছেড়ে দিয়ে পরের প্রশ্নে মনোযোগ দিন।

blocks.text: Panic is attention pointed at fear instead of at the next answer. The cure is not “calm down,” which is useless advice under pressure; the cure is an immediate, concrete task — eyes go to the next question, ear starts hunting the next target. Action displaces panic.
The expert listening mindset, in slow motion

In the pause before a part begins, the expert turns each question into a “listen for” target: for a form, they note name (spelling), number (digits), cost (money, maybe called “fee”), and build a small mental queue of what is coming and in what order.

In the first seconds of the audio, they orient — who is speaking, what is the situation — without grabbing at the opening lines in fear, since Part 1 answers rarely arrive immediately. As each answer approaches, attention sharpens the instant a signpost or paraphrase appears, and the answer is written immediately, in rough form, without losing pace.

When a correction or distractor appears, the expert does not flinch; they expected it, and overwrite the bait without hesitation. When they miss one, there is a flicker of recognition, then nothing — eyes are already on the next question. Underneath it all is a quiet confidence built entirely on preparation, not talent.
Expert thinking: the same moment, three heads
A form-completion form asks for a “daily rate,” and the audio says: “It's normally forty pounds a night, but for members it comes down to thirty-two.”

items: What a beginner thinks: “Forty pounds. There it is.” Writes 40, relaxes, misses that the answer changed, and has stopped listening as “thirty-two” goes past.
What an experienced student thinks: “Two numbers. There is a ‘but,’ so the second one probably matters.” Writes 32, correctly, but a beat behind going into the next question.

What an expert candidate notices: before the audio, they saw the gap said “member rate,” not just “rate,” so when “for members” arrived the bell was already ringing. They were never tempted by 40 at all, and are already reading the next question.

blocks.text: The gap between these three is not English. It is preparation and expectation. Everything in this module is designed to move you into the third head.
Practice

Strategy without practice is entertainment. These first drills are Level 1 (understand) and Level 2 (guided). There is no audio here; these train the thinking that must happen before you ever press play.
Drill 1.1 (Level 1): Name the mode

blocks.label: Drill 1.1 (Level 1): Name the mode
blocks.prompt:
For each question type, decide whether you should be listening for specific information (SI) or for meaning (M).
1. Form completion, gap for a phone number.
2. Multiple choice: “What does the woman think about the new timetable?”
3. Table completion, gap for a price.
4. Matching: match each speaker to their opinion.
5. Note completion, gap for a place name.
6. Multiple choice: “Why did the project change direction?”
blocks.answer:
1. SI — a phone number is a pure fact; narrow, precise ear, digits only.
2. M — an opinion needs a wide ear that follows attitude, not a single word.
3. SI — a price is a fact; wait for money.
4. M — matching opinions means tracking what each person believes, and in Part 3 also who is speaking.
5. SI — a place name is a fact, though watch the spelling.
6. M — reasoning and cause, not a single stated fact.
The lesson: you can tell from the question, before any audio, whether to set your ear narrow or wide.

blocks.text: Drill 1.2 (Level 2): Spot the correction

blocks.label: Drill 1.2 (Level 2): Spot the correction
blocks.prompt:
In each line, the answer changes. Underline the signal word, then write the correct answer.
1. “The talk is in Hall B, sorry, Hall D.”
2. “We open at nine, though on Saturdays it's actually ten.”
3. “Post it to 15 Mill Road, no wait, 50 Mill Road.”
4. “I was going to say Tuesday, but let's make it Friday.”
5. “The fee is fifteen pounds, or twelve if you book online, and most people book online.”
blocks.answer:
1. Signal: sorry. Answer: Hall D.
2. Signal: though / actually. Answer for Saturday: ten (the answer depends on the condition).
3. Signal: no wait. Answer: 50 Mill Road.
4. Signal: but. Answer: Friday.
5. Signal: or / “most people book online.” Answer: twelve — not every distractor uses sorry/but; sometimes the speaker steers you with a comment. Read the whole sentence before committing.
Lesson: corrections and choices are signalled by small words (sorry, no, wait, but, actually, though, or). Treat these as alarms that say the real answer is near.

blocks.text: Drill 1.3 (Level 2): Predict the shape

blocks.label: Drill 1.3 (Level 2): Predict the shape
blocks.prompt:
For each gap, write what shape of answer you expect (number, date, time, name, singular noun, plural noun, place).
1. “Membership costs ____ per year.”
2. “The tour leaves from the ____ entrance.”
3. “You should bring ____ and ____.” (two items)
4. “The museum was founded in ____.”
5. “Ask for ____ at the front desk.” (a person)
blocks.answer:
1. Number (an amount of money). Listen for currency.
2. Singular noun / place word (main, side, north, rear).
3. Two plural or singular nouns; the question needs two answers, so do not stop after the first.
4. A year (a date); listen for a four-digit year.
5. A name (a person or department); likely spelled or clearly stated.
Lesson: predicting the shape narrows your ear before the flood arrives. This prediction habit is the backbone of the next chapter.

chapters.title: File 02: Prediction, Keywords, and Paraphrase Recognition
chapters.summary: The engine of Listening: predicting the shape of each gap, choosing anchor keywords the exam cannot disguise, and pre-loading likely paraphrases before the audio plays.

blocks.text: These three skills are the engine of Listening. Prediction tells your ear what to wait for. Keywords tell your eyes where to wait. Paraphrase recognition tells you what the answer will sound like when it arrives, because it will almost never arrive in the words you expect. Master these three and half of the Listening test is already won before the audio starts.
PART 3
Question Prediction

Prediction is the habit that most separates a Band 8 candidate from a Band 6 one, and almost nobody teaches it properly. The beginner reads a question and waits. The expert reads a question and knows what is coming.

Ask, of every single gap before the audio begins: “What kind of answer am I about to hear?” That question sets a filter in your mind, and that filter is what lets you catch one word out of a flood of two hundred.

Predict on two layers. Layer 1 is the grammatical shape: is the missing word a noun, verb, adjective, or number? You can nearly always tell from the words around the gap (“open until ____” needs a time; “must not ____ inside” needs a verb; “surprisingly ____” needs an adjective; “bring your own ____” needs a countable noun). Layer 2 is the information type: name, place, measurement, date, price, object, role.

rows: Often spelled out; listen letter by letter
A concrete noun; check singular or plural
What someone does, must do, or must avoid
A describing word about quality or attitude

blocks.text: Read around the gap, not just up to it. Beginners read only the words before a gap; experts read the words after it too, because the word after the gap often fixes the grammar and narrows the meaning far more than the word before. “The museum's ____ collection attracts thousands of visitors” only becomes predictable once you read past the gap to “collection,” which tells you the answer is an adjective or noun describing a type of collection.

Predict singular or plural too, since the words around a gap often reveal it (“there is a ____” forces singular; “guests are given two ____” forces plural; “each room has its own ____” forces singular). This is not only about catching the answer; a mismatch between what you predicted and what you caught is a useful alarm that you misheard.

Respect the word limit before you write. Every completion task has an instruction such as “Write ONE WORD ONLY” or “NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER.” Writing three words where two are allowed makes the answer wrong even if the meaning is perfect. Predict the length too, and do not cram in extra describing words the speaker uses if the limit is one word.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: A hyphenated word (part-time, twenty-five, check-in) counts as one word. Numbers written as figures (25, 1990) count as a number, not a word. Knowing this frees you to write “part-time” under a one-word limit without fear.
blocks.bn: হাইফেন দেওয়া শব্দ (part-time) একটি শব্দ হিসেবে গণ্য হয়। সংখ্যা অঙ্কে লিখলে (25) সেটা শব্দ নয়, সংখ্যা হিসেবে ধরা হয়।

blocks.text: Worked example: a note-completion set asks for Name, Number of nights, Room type ____ room, Extra charge for ____. Predicting aloud, the expert thinks: a surname, probably spelled; a small number; a short adjective before “room” (single, double, standard, deluxe); a noun for something paid extra (breakfast, parking, wifi, a pet). Four tight nets set in fifteen seconds — now each answer drops into the net waiting for it while the surrounding chatter slides past unnoticed.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: If you finish predicting a set of gaps before the audio starts, do not sit idle. Read ahead into the next set. The pauses are never quite long enough for the slow reader, so the fast predictor banks time and reads into the future.
blocks.bn: প্রশ্ন পড়া শেষ হলে বসে থাকবেন না, পরের সেটা আগেভাগে পড়ে রাখুন। বিরতি কখনওই যথেষ্ট লম্বা হয় না।

blocks.text: PART 4
Keywords

Ask a struggling candidate to prepare a question and watch what they do: they underline almost every word. An underline on everything is an underline on nothing. Keyword skill is about choosing the few words that will actually help you find the answer, and ignoring the rest.

Not all words are equal. Strong keywords carry the specific meaning of the question (unusual nouns, specific verbs, the topic). Weak keywords are common, low-information words (the, a, some, thing, people) that point nowhere. Unique keywords are unlikely to appear anywhere else in the passage (a proper name, a number, a technical term) and are the most valuable of all. Generic keywords are broad and locate poorly (problem, change, area). Concept keywords carry an idea rather than a word and warn you a paraphrase is coming.

Names, numbers, and dates are almost never paraphrased. Content words almost always are. So your best anchors are the words the exam cannot change: it can turn “cheap” into “won't break the bank,” but it cannot turn the year 1985 into anything except 1985.

Your keyword priority order: 1) unique anchors that cannot change (names, numbers, dates, technical terms) — mark first; 2) strong content words that carry the meaning — mark, but expect them to be paraphrased; 3) concept words that warn a paraphrase is coming — note mentally; 4) weak and generic words — ignore.

Worked example: “In 1996, the company moved its headquarters to ____.” The strongest keyword is 1996, an anchor that cannot be paraphrased. When you hear “in ninety-six,” you know the answer is arriving right now, even if “headquarters” and “moved” are reworded as “relocated its main offices.”

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: When a question contains a number or a name, that is usually your single best keyword. Circle it and relax about the rest. The exam gave you a word it is not allowed to disguise.
blocks.bn: প্রশ্নে সংখ্যা বা নাম থাকলে সেটাই সাধারণত সবচেয়ে ভালো keyword, কারণ পরীক্ষা সেটা বদলাতে পারে না।

blocks.text: PART 5
Paraphrase Recognition

This is the deepest chapter in the module, because paraphrase is the mechanism the whole test runs on. Understand it fully and the exam stops feeling like a trap and starts feeling like a translation you can do.

The question and the audio carry the same meaning in different words. The exam is testing whether you can recognise meaning across changed wording. It is not testing whether you can hear a matching word.

The forms paraphrase takes: (1) synonym — cost becomes price/fee/charge; (2) word-class change — “the decision to close” becomes “they decided to close”; (3) active/passive swap — “the council built the bridge” becomes “the bridge was built by the council”; (4) expression or description — “cheap” becomes “won't break the bank”; (5) indirect wording — the answer is implied rather than stated directly; (6) numerical paraphrase — 50% becomes “half”, doubled becomes “twice as many”; (7) conceptual paraphrase — the whole idea is rebuilt with no shared words at all.

Predict the paraphrase before you listen: this is where prediction and paraphrase meet, and it is the highest-value drill in the module. Take your strong keyword and ask, “If the exam does not use this word, how else might they say it?” Spend two seconds generating alternatives, so your ear is ready for any of them when the paraphrase arrives.

Expert thinking: the question says “The main disadvantage of the site was its ____,” and the audio says “The one real drawback with the location was how far it sat from the station.” A beginner waits to hear the word “disadvantage” and never does, missing the whole sentence. An experienced student catches “drawback” as a match but is a beat late. An expert candidate had already pre-loaded disadvantage = drawback/downside/problem/negative, so “drawback” landed with zero delay and “location” was clearly “site” paraphrased; the answer, distance from the station, was caught cleanly. The expert did not hear better — they expected better.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: The words most likely to be paraphrased are the content words in the question. The words least likely to change are names, numbers, and dates. Listen for the meaning of the content words and the sound of the fixed words.
blocks.bn: প্রশ্নের অর্থবহ শব্দগুলো বদলে যাওয়ার সম্ভাবনা বেশি; নাম, সংখ্যা, তারিখ বদলায় না।

blocks.text: Practice
Drill 2.1 (Level 1): What shape is the answer?

blocks.label: Drill 2.1 (Level 1): What shape is the answer?
blocks.prompt:
For each gap, write the grammatical shape (noun, verb, adjective, number) and the information type.
1. “The next train departs at ____.”
2. “Please do not ____ the exhibits.”
3. “The workshop is held every ____.” (a day)
4. “Membership costs ____ a month.”
5. “Wear ____ shoes for the walk.”
6. “Leave your bag at the ____ desk.”
blocks.answer:
1. Number, a time. 2. Verb: touch, photograph, lean on. 3. Noun, a day of the week. 4. Number, a price. 5. Adjective (comfortable, sturdy, waterproof). 6. Noun/role word before “desk” (reception, information, front).
Lesson: every gap tells you its own shape if you read both sides of it.

blocks.text: Drill 2.2 (Level 2): Choose the best keyword

blocks.label: Drill 2.2 (Level 2): Choose the best keyword
blocks.prompt:
For each question, underline the ONE word you would rely on to locate the answer, and say what type it is (unique anchor, strong content, concept).
1. “How much does the annual pass cost?”
2. “In 2010, the factory switched to solar power.”
3. “The main difficulty with the plan was funding.”
4. “Passengers should report to Professor Nolan.”
5. “The village is famous for its cheese.”
blocks.answer:
1. cost — strong content, likely paraphrased to price/how much.
2. 2010 — unique anchor, cannot change.
3. funding/difficulty — concept; expect the paraphrase “the hard part,” “money.”
4. Nolan — unique anchor, a name.
5. cheese — strong, fairly unique content word.
Lesson: a name, number, or date in the question usually wins as your keyword.

blocks.text: Drill 2.3 (Level 2): Predict the paraphrase

blocks.label: Drill 2.3 (Level 2): Predict the paraphrase
blocks.prompt: For each keyword, write two or three ways the audio might reword it: buy, dangerous, increase, nearby, important, children.
blocks.answer:
buy: purchase, pick up, pay for. dangerous: risky, unsafe, hazardous. increase: rise, go up, climb. nearby: close by, within walking distance, a short way off. important: crucial, vital, key, essential. children: kids, youngsters, the young.
Lesson: doing this for two seconds per keyword before the audio is exactly what turns a surprise into an expected event.

blocks.text: Drill 2.4 (Level 3): Match the paraphrase

blocks.label: Drill 2.4 (Level 3): Match the paraphrase
blocks.prompt:
Match each question phrase (1–6) to the audio phrase (A–F) that carries the same meaning.
Questions: 1. cheap to run 2. difficult to find 3. the decision to expand 4. built in 1990 5. very popular 6. close to the coast
Audio: A. “they chose to grow the business” B. “always packed with visitors” C. “dates back to nineteen ninety” D. “costs very little to keep going” E. “just a short drive from the sea” F. “not easy to track down”
blocks.answer:
1→D, 2→F, 3→A (note the word-class change: decision→chose, expand→grow), 4→C (the fixed number survives unchanged), 5→B, 6→E.
Lesson: in every pair the meaning is identical while the words are almost entirely different. Train your mind to hear meaning, not words.

chapters.title: File 03: Signposting and the Distractor Masterclass
chapters.summary: The signal-to-meaning map, the contrast/correction shape that hides most answers, all fourteen distractor types with defuses, and the distractor defusing checklist.

blocks.text: These two chapters belong together. Signposts are the words the speaker uses to guide you towards the answer. Distractors are the ways the exam uses those same words to guide you away from it. Learn both sides of the same coin and you will stop being surprised by the recording, because you will hear the machinery working.
PART 6
Signposting

A signpost is a small word or phrase that tells you what the speaker is about to do: add a point, change direction, correct themselves, give a reason, or reach a conclusion. In Listening you cannot see structure on a page, so signposts are your only map.

Signposts win marks for two reasons. First, they tell you where the answer is (“the main thing to remember is” means the answer is in the next breath; “but actually” means the previous information has just been cancelled). Second, they keep you oriented in long stretches of speech, since in Part 4 a lecture can run for minutes without a pause.

rows: first, firstly, to begin with, then, next, after that
also, in addition, another thing, as well as
often a second answer in a list
but, however, although, on the other hand
the real point is usually the second half
actually, in fact, to be honest
sorry, no, I mean, or rather, let me change that
the answer is what comes after
instead, rather than, as opposed to
the main reason, the key point, importantly
because, since, so, as a result, that is why
a reason or a consequence answer
finally, lastly, to sum up, overall, in the end

moving on, turning to, as for

blocks.text: The two most valuable signal families are contrast (but, however) and correction (sorry, actually, I mean), because the exam's favourite way to hide an answer follows the same shape every time: [wrong or old information] + [signal] + [right or new information]. “We usually meet in the library, but this week it's in Room 12” — the decoy is the library, but is the signal, Room 12 is the answer.

In Part 3, with several speakers, signposts do an extra job: they mark who agrees, who disagrees, and who changes their mind (“I'm not so sure,” “that's a fair point, but,” “I used to think so, though now”). Since Part 3 questions frequently ask what a specific person thinks, catching these shifts is the whole game.

Worked example: a Part 2 note asks for the café's closing time and a free item. Audio: “The café is open all day, closing at five, though on Fridays it stays open until eight. And if you need it, just ask at the desk for a free audio guide.” For the closing time, the signal “though on Fridays” tells you eight is a special case; unless the question specifies Friday, the answer is five — the decoy was the later, more memorable number. For the free item, “just ask at the desk for a free ____” lands the answer directly: audio guide.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: Train yourself to physically react to the words but, actually, however, sorry, and instead. The moment one lands, assume any answer you were about to write is now the decoy, and wait for the correction.
blocks.bn: but, actually, however, sorry, instead এই শব্দগুলো শুনলেই সতর্ক হয়ে যান। এর আগে যা শুনেছেন সেটা সাধারণত ফাঁদ, আসল উত্তর এই শব্দের পরে আসে।

blocks.text: PART 7
The Distractor Masterclass

“I heard it, but it was not the answer.” This is the largest chapter in the Listening module, because distractors are how the exam separates a Band 6 listener from a Band 8 one. Both hear the same words; only one knows which are bait.

Hearing a word is not the same as that word being the answer. The exam deliberately says the wrong option out loud so that a passive listener will grab it. Every distractor in the test is a variation of this one move.
Fourteen forms the distractor takes, each with what it looks like, why students fall for it, and how to defuse it:

items: 1. The correction — “Room 214, sorry, 240.” Defuse: never write and relax; treat sorry/no/I mean/actually as an instruction to overwrite.
2. Two numbers — “fifty pounds last year, but sixty now.” Defuse: expect more than one number when you predicted a number; listen for the condition that selects the right one.
3. Two dates — opened vs. extended. Defuse: match the date to the exact thing the question asks about.
4. Two times — start time vs. arrival time vs. closing time. Defuse: tie each time to its own action.
5. Two locations — old place vs. new place. Defuse: the signpost (now, these days, instead) tells you the current one, usually the answer.
6. Two names — the primary contact vs. the backup “if he's away.” Defuse: listen for the condition that applies.
7. Similar options (multiple choice) — both A and B discussed before one is chosen. Defuse: mention is not endorsement; wait for the verdict.
8. Related information — lots of true detail, only some of which fits the gap. Defuse: hold the exact question in mind; relevance is not the same as being the answer.
9. The example trap — general category vs. one example (“warm clothing… hat, gloves, scarf”). Defuse: check whether the gap wants the category or the specific item; the word limit often tells you.
10. Opinion versus fact — a fact stated, then an opinion about it. Defuse: decide from the question which one you need before the audio.
11. Speaker disagreement (Part 3) — catching the opinion but attaching it to the wrong speaker. Defuse: track voices, not just views.
12. The changed decision — the group agrees, then reverses it. Defuse: wait for the group to settle; the last agreed version is the answer.
13. The rejected option — “we considered a boat trip, but in the end we ruled it out.” Defuse: listen for the rejection frame; a mentioned option is often a rejected option.
14. The negative or hedge trap — a small “not” flips the meaning (“the morning session isn't the busy one”). Defuse: listen for negation as carefully as for content.

blocks.text: Expert thinking: a multiple-choice question asks when the speaker recommends visiting a castle, with options summer, spring, winter. The audio criticises summer and spring in turn before praising winter with “if you ask me” and “I always tell people.” A beginner picks A the instant “summer” is heard, confusing “most people come” with a recommendation. An experienced student gets to C but was briefly tempted by each option along the way. An expert candidate knew beforehand that all three options are usually named, so listened only for the verdict words and was never tempted — they expected the decoys because they knew the decoys would come.

The distractor defusing checklist, to run silently on any answer you are unsure of: 1) Did the speaker finish the thought, or might a correction still come? 2) Was there a signal word that cancels what I heard? 3) Does this detail answer the exact thing the question asks, or just something related? 4) In multiple choice, did the speaker endorse this option, or merely mention it? 5) Was there a “not” or a rejection I might have missed? 6) In Part 3, am I sure which speaker said this? If any answer is uncertain, wait one more clause before committing.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: The exam almost always says the wrong answer out loud before it says the right one. So the first plausible thing you hear is, more often than not, the decoy. Slow your trigger finger by one clause and most distractors disappear.
blocks.bn: পরীক্ষা সাধারণত সঠিক উত্তরের আগে ভুল উত্তরটি বলে দেয়। একটু ধৈর্য ধরুন, বাক্যটা শেষ হতে দিন।

blocks.text: Practice
Drill 3.1 (Level 2): Name the signal

blocks.label: Drill 3.1 (Level 2): Name the signal
blocks.prompt:
Underline the signpost and say what it predicts (new point, contrast, correction, importance, conclusion).
1. “To begin with, the museum was quite small.”
2. “The talk is in Room 5, sorry, Room 9.”
3. “The key thing to remember is your ticket number.”
4. “It's cheaper online, however delivery takes longer.”
5. “So, overall, the project was a success.”
blocks.answer:
1. “To begin with” — new point, first in a sequence.
2. “Sorry” — correction; Room 9 replaces Room 5.
3. “The key thing to remember” — importance; the answer is right here.
4. “However” — contrast; the catch follows the benefit.
5. “So, overall” — conclusion; a summary point follows.
Lesson: the signal tells you what to do with the surrounding words before you even process their meaning.

blocks.text: Drill 3.2 (Level 4): Find the real answer

blocks.label: Drill 3.2 (Level 4): Find the real answer (correction and choice)
blocks.prompt:
Each line hides a decoy and an answer. Write the answer only.
1. “Send it to the Oxford office, no, the Cambridge one now handles bookings.”
2. “The deposit is a hundred pounds, though students pay just fifty.”
3. “We'll meet at the station, actually let's make it the car park, it's easier.”
4. “The lecture's usually on Monday, but this week it's been moved to Thursday.”
5. “You'll be shown around by Dr Adams, or by his assistant if he's teaching.”
6. “It holds about two hundred people, well, closer to two fifty since the refit.”
blocks.answer:
1. Cambridge. 2. Fifty (for students; read the gap's condition). 3. Car park. 4. Thursday. 5. Dr Adams normally, or the assistant “if he's teaching” — depends on the condition in the question. 6. Two fifty (250).
Lesson: in every case the answer sat after a signal word and the decoy sat before it — the shape of nearly every correction trap.

blocks.text: Drill 3.3 (Level 4): Multiple-choice verdict

blocks.label: Drill 3.3 (Level 4): Multiple-choice verdict
blocks.prompt:
For each, decide which option the speaker actually recommends.
1. Options: bus / train / car. Audio: “The bus is cheap but slow, and the train's pricey. The car gives you freedom, so that's what I'd suggest.”
2. Options: morning / afternoon / evening. Audio: “Mornings get crowded, evenings can be cold, so aim for the afternoon.”
3. Options: cotton / wool / synthetic. Audio: “Cotton's comfortable, and synthetic dries fast, but for warmth nothing beats wool, which is what I recommend for this trip.”
blocks.answer:
1. Car — the bus and train are named and criticised; “that's what I'd suggest” is the verdict.
2. Afternoon — morning and evening are dismissed; what remains is the recommendation.
3. Wool — cotton and synthetic get positive-sounding mentions, the trap; “nothing beats wool, which is what I recommend” is the verdict.
Lesson: mention is not endorsement. Listen only for the verdict words.

blocks.text: Drill 3.4 (Level 4): Rejected option and negation

blocks.label: Drill 3.4 (Level 4): Rejected option and negation
blocks.prompt:
Write what the group or speaker actually chose or meant.
1. “We thought about hiring a hall, but we ruled it out and booked the community centre instead.”
2. “It isn't the ground floor that floods; it's the basement.”
3. “Some suggested a written test, though in the end we went with an interview.”
4. “The problem wasn't the cost, it was finding the time.”
blocks.answer:
1. Community centre — the hall was rejected. 2. The basement floods — the “isn't” removes the ground floor. 3. An interview — the written test was rejected. 4. Finding the time — the real issue follows “it was.”
Lesson: a mentioned option is frequently a rejected option, and a single “not” can flip the entire meaning.

blocks.text: Drill 3.5 (Level 3): Part 3 opinion tracking

blocks.label: Drill 3.5 (Level 3): Part 3 opinion tracking
blocks.prompt:
Read the exchange and answer the question.
Tutor: “What did you make of the reading?” Maya: “I found the methodology weak, too few participants.” Sam: “Really? I thought that was its strength, small but detailed.” Maya: “Hmm, when you put it that way, maybe you have a point.”
Question: What does Maya finally think about the number of participants?
blocks.answer:
Maya finally thinks the small number of participants may be a strength, not a weakness — she concedes Sam's point. Her first view (too few, a weakness) is the decoy; “when you put it that way, maybe you have a point” marks her change of mind.
Lesson: in Part 3, first opinions are often reversed. Track each speaker and wait for the exchange to settle.

chapters.title: File 04: Every Question Type, Part One: The Completion Family
chapters.summary: Form, note, table, flow-chart, summary, and sentence completion — how to recognise each, what to predict, where the answer sits, the traps, and worked examples.

blocks.text: The twelve Listening question types fall into natural groups. This file covers the six completion types, where you write a missing word or number into a gap: form, note, table, flow-chart, summary, and sentence completion. They share one engine, the prediction and paraphrase skills from File 02, and one discipline, the word limit.
1. Form completion

Recognise it: a form with labelled fields (Name, Address, Date, Phone). Almost always Part 1, usually the first thing you meet in the whole test. What it tests: catching concrete personal and factual details in real speech — listening for specific information at its purest.

Before the audio: read every field label and turn each into a prediction, noting the word limit. Predict and listen for: the exact type each field needs; brace for spelling on names and addresses; be ready for corrections on numbers. Where the answer sits: in order, one field at a time, and the “writer” often repeats the detail back, giving a second chance to confirm.

Traps: corrections, spelled names with tricky letters, numbers stated then adjusted, postcodes mixing letters and digits. Beginner mistake: writing the first thing heard and relaxing, then missing the correction, or panicking at spelling and losing the next field. Expert approach: predicts every field, writes fast and rough, keeps one eye on the next field.

Worked example: Surname ____, Arrival date ____, Number of nights ____. Audio: “It's Hendricks, H-E-N-D-R-I-C-K-S… The fourteenth of March… Three, no sorry, four nights.” Answers: Hendricks; 14 March; four (not three — caught by “no sorry”).

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: In Part 1, expect names and reference codes to be spelled out. Do not guess the spelling from the sound; wait for the letters and write them as they come. Common trap letters are pairs that sound alike: m/n, b/p, and the vowel e said the British way.
blocks.bn: Part 1-এ নাম আর কোড প্রায়ই বানান করে বলা হয়। শব্দ শুনে অনুমান করবেন না, অক্ষরগুলো শুনে লিখুন। m/n, b/p এই জোড়াগুলো শুনতে একরকম, সাবধান।

blocks.text: 2. Note completion

Recognise it: a skeleton of notes under a title, often with headings and bullet gaps, laid out the way someone would jot a talk. Common in Parts 2 and 4. What it tests: following the structure of a talk and pulling out key details as the speaker moves through their points.

Before the audio: read the headings first, then the gaps — headings tell you the shape of the talk and where you are at any moment. Predict and listen for: the speaker's signposting lines up with your headings; when the topic changes, move with them. Where the answer sits: in order, under each heading in turn.

Traps: extra true detail that does not fit the specific note; paraphrase between heading word and audio; losing your place when a speaker lingers. Beginner mistake: reading the notes as continuous prose and getting lost. Expert approach: uses headings as anchors, predicts the gap shape, and writes only the word that fits.

Worked example: The town museum — Opened: originally a ____; Best-known exhibit: a Roman ____. Audio: “The building started life as a flour mill before becoming a museum in the 1970s. Its most famous piece… is a beautifully preserved Roman helmet.” Answers: flour mill; helmet.
3. Table completion
Recognise it: a grid with rows and columns and some cells empty. What it tests: tracking information along two dimensions at once and slotting each detail into the right cell.

Before the audio: read the row and column headers first — they tell you the categories the speaker will move through. Predict and listen for: the direction the table fills (usually row by row), and the header words or their paraphrases that cue each cell. Where the answer sits: left to right, top to bottom, matching the speaker's progression.

Traps: jumping to the wrong cell because two rows discuss similar things; numbers that belong to a neighbouring cell; comparisons mentioning several cells' worth of data in one sentence. Beginner mistake: losing which row is being discussed, so one slip corrupts several answers. Expert approach: keeps a mental finger on the current cell and moves it deliberately.

Worked example: Pottery / Tuesday / ____ (cost); Drawing / ____ (day) / 40 pounds. Audio: “Pottery runs on Tuesdays and costs fifty pounds. Drawing is a bit cheaper at forty, and that one's on Thursdays.” Answers: 50 pounds; Thursday.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: In tables, the headers are your safety rail. If you ever feel lost, snap your eyes back to the row and column headers rather than to the gap itself. They re-anchor you faster than rereading the empty cell.
blocks.bn: তেবিলে row আর column-এর হেডিং হলো আপনার নিরাপত্তা রেলিং। হারিয়ে গেলে ফাঁকা ঘরের দিকে না তাকিয়ে হেডিংে দেখুন।

blocks.text: 4. Flow-chart completion
Recognise it: boxes connected by arrows showing the stages of a process, with some boxes to complete. What it tests: following a described process in order and identifying each stage or action.

Before the audio: read the whole chart top to bottom so you understand the process before it is described. Predict and listen for: sequence language (first, then, next, after that, once this is done, finally); whether each gap is an action (verb-led) or a thing (noun-led). Where the answer sits: strictly in order, following the arrows.

Traps: steps mentioned then reordered (“but before that, you need to”); extra sub-steps that are not boxes; paraphrase of action words. Beginner mistake: treating each box in isolation and missing when the speaker doubles back. Expert approach: rides the sequence words and stays alert for order-adjusting phrases.

Worked example: Collect form → ____ → Submit to office → ____. Audio: “First you collect the form. Then you'll need to get it signed by your supervisor before you submit it. After submitting, you simply wait for confirmation by email.” Answers: get it signed; wait for confirmation.
5. Summary completion

Recognise it: a paragraph that summarises part of the recording with several gaps, sometimes filled from a word box. What it tests: following a stretch of the talk and capturing its key content words while the summary itself is paraphrased.

Before the audio: read the whole summary first so you know the overall meaning, then predict each gap; expect the surrounding words not to match the audio exactly. Predict and listen for: the part of speech, then the audio word that completes the paraphrased sense. Where the answer sits: usually in order across the summarised section.

Traps: with a word box, there are always more options than gaps, and the extras are plausible-sounding distractors. Beginner mistake: trying to match the summary's exact words in the audio and hearing nothing. Expert approach: reads for meaning and, with a box, eliminates by grammar first, then meaning.

Worked example: “The scheme was first introduced to reduce ____ in the city centre, and proved most popular with ____.” Audio: “The initiative began as a way of cutting down on traffic congestion downtown, and interestingly it was the elderly who took it up most enthusiastically.” Answers: congestion; the elderly.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: When summary completion gives you a box of words, count the options against the gaps. There are always more words than gaps, and the spare words are traps built to fit the topic but not the sentence. Eliminate by grammar before you decide by meaning.
blocks.bn: Summary completion-এ শব্দের বাক্স দিলে গুনে দেখুন, ফাঁকের চেয়ে শব্দ বেশি থাকে। আগে ব্যাকরণ দিয়ে বাদ দিন, পরে অর্থ দিয়ে বাছুন।

blocks.text: 6. Sentence completion

Recognise it: a list of separate sentences, each with a gap, completed with words from the recording. Unlike a summary, the sentences do not form one flowing paragraph. What it tests: catching specific information and fitting it grammatically into a given sentence frame.

Before the audio: read each sentence and predict the gap's part of speech and meaning; the fixed half of the sentence often contains the keyword that will be paraphrased. Where the answer sits: in order down the list, matching the recording's progression.

Traps: grammatical mismatches (a phrase that means the right thing but does not fit the sentence); over-length answers; related detail that fits the topic but not the exact sentence. Beginner mistake: writing a whole heard phrase without checking it slots grammatically, or exceeding the word limit. Expert approach: treats the sentence frame as a template and reads the completed sentence back in their head to check it makes sense.

Worked example: “The new policy was designed to help ____ find affordable housing.” Audio: “The whole point of the reform was to give first-time buyers a realistic chance of getting onto the property ladder without being priced out.” Answer: first-time buyers.
Practice
Drill 4.1 (Level 2): Predict before you listen

blocks.label: Drill 4.1 (Level 2): Predict before you listen
blocks.prompt:
For each gap, write the part of speech and information type you expect.
1. Form: “Membership type: ____”
2. Note: “Founded in ____”
3. Table cell under “Price”: ____
4. Flow-chart: “____ the mixture” (a box)
5. Summary: “…which led to a sharp ____ in sales.”
6. Sentence: “Students must bring their own ____.”
blocks.answer:
1. Noun/category word (individual, family, student). 2. A number, a year. 3. A number, a price. 4. A verb (stir, heat, pour). 5. A noun — given “sharp,” probably rise/fall/increase/drop. 6. A noun, a countable object; check singular or plural.
Lesson: predicting the part of speech first prevents the most common completion error.

blocks.text: Drill 4.2 (Level 3): Catch the answer

blocks.label: Drill 4.2 (Level 3): Catch the answer
blocks.prompt:
Read each transcript once and write the answer within the word limit shown.
1. (ONE WORD) “The tour is not suitable for ____.” — “We'd advise against bringing very young children on this particular tour.”
2. (ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER) “Deposit: ____.” — “You'll need to leave a deposit, that's twenty pounds, refundable when you return the key.”
3. (TWO WORDS) “Main problem reported: ____.” — “The single biggest complaint we get, by a long way, is the poor lighting in the car park.”
4. (ONE WORD) “The material is valued for being lightweight and ____.” — “What makes it so useful is that it's both very light and surprisingly durable.”
blocks.answer:
1. children. 2. 20 (pounds). 3. poor lighting. 4. durable.
Lesson: in every item the audio reworded the sentence's keyword. You found the answer by tracking meaning, not by matching words.

blocks.text: Drill 4.3 (Level 4): Beat the trap

blocks.label: Drill 4.3 (Level 4): Beat the trap
blocks.prompt:
Each transcript hides a distractor. Write the correct answer.
1. Table, cost cell for “Adult ticket”: ____. “Adult tickets are twelve pounds, though it's eight for children and concessions.”
2. Flow-chart: “Then ____.” (the step immediately after heating) “After heating the solution, you filter it. Oh, but before filtering, remember to let it cool completely.”
3. Sentence (ONE WORD): “The festival was cancelled because of ____.” “They'd worried about funding all year, but in the end it was the weather that forced them to call it off.”
4. Summary (box: rural / urban / coastal): “The scheme worked best in ____ areas.” “It struggled in the big cities but really thrived out in the countryside.”
blocks.answer:
1. 12 pounds — match the number to the exact row; eight is the child/concession decoy.
2. filter it — the gap asked for the step immediately after heating, which is filtering; “before filtering… let it cool” inserts an earlier step, it does not replace this one.
3. weather — funding was the year-long worry (decoy); “but in the end” flips it.
4. rural — “out in the countryside” paraphrases rural; “big cities” is the urban decoy.
Lesson: completion answers live inside the same distractor machinery from File 03.

chapters.title: File 05: Every Question Type, Part Two: Selection and Matching
chapters.summary: Multiple choice, multiple-answer, matching, map labelling, diagram labelling, and short answer — deciding between options rather than catching a word, and the traps unique to each.

blocks.text: This file covers the remaining six Listening question types: multiple choice, multiple-answer, matching, map labelling, diagram labelling, and short answer. Unlike the completion family, where you catch a word and write it, these types ask you to choose or place — shifting the skill from catching to deciding, and bringing a different set of traps.
7. Multiple choice (choose one)

Recognise it: a question stem followed by three options, A, B, C. What it tests: detailed understanding, often of an opinion, reason, or gist — harder because all three options are usually mentioned in the audio.

Before the audio: read the stem and all three options; understand how they differ, since that difference is what you are really listening for. During the audio: expect language connected to all three options by design; do not choose just because you heard its words — wait for the speaker's verdict words (I think, in the end, what matters most, so we chose).

Traps: two-option and similar-option distractors; an option mentioned then rejected. Beginner mistake: selects the option whose words arrive first. Expert approach: treats every option as “mentioned until endorsed.”

Worked example: “Why did the team change suppliers?” A) price B) quality C) delivery times. Audio: “The old supplier was actually cheaper, and the quality was fine, but they kept missing deadlines, and that's ultimately why we switched.” Answer: C — price and quality are decoys; “kept missing deadlines” paraphrases delivery times, confirmed by the verdict phrase.
8. Multiple-answer (choose two or more)
Recognise it: “Which TWO things does the speaker mention?” with a longer option list. What it tests: catching several correct items scattered among distractors.

Before the audio: read all options and turn each into a concept to listen for; three of five will be decoys. During the audio: the two answers may not sit next to each other and rarely arrive in list order; keep all options live and tick a match only when clearly affirmed.

Traps: an option mentioned but denied (“we thought about a gym, but decided not to”); two similar-sounding options where only one is affirmed. Beginner mistake: picks the first two options discussed regardless of affirmation. Expert approach: waits for clear affirmation of each item.

Worked example: “Which TWO facilities are new this year?” A) café B) car park C) library D) gym E) garden. Audio: “We've always had the café and the library. This year we finally added a car park, and the garden is brand new too. A gym was requested but hasn't happened yet.” Answers: B and E — café/library are old, gym was rejected.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: In choose-two questions, listen as hard for the word “not” and for rejection frames as for the items themselves. The exam loves to name a tempting option and then quietly cancel it. A denied option is a wrong answer wearing the costume of a right one.
blocks.bn: দুটি বেছে নিন প্রশ্নে not এবং বাতিল করা শব্দগুলো (decided not to, hasn't happened) খুব মন দিয়ে শুনুন।

blocks.text: 9. Matching

Recognise it: a list of items matched against a set of options, often lettered. What it tests: detailed listening while tracking several threads at once — common in Part 3, matching speakers to views.

Before the audio: read the item list and option box; notice if options can repeat; understand each option's meaning, since you will hear meaning, not words. During the audio: items are usually discussed in order, but options jump around; hold their meanings ready and assign as each item is discussed.

Traps: options worded so more than one seems to fit; an opinion voiced by one person and agreed with by another. Beginner mistake: loses track of which item is being discussed, or attaches an opinion to whoever spoke last. Expert approach: keeps a finger on the current item and tracks each speaker by name.

Worked example: match each person to their view of a new timetable (i. too rushed, ii. an improvement, iii. confusing). “Ben: I actually like it, it's much better than before. Priya: I find it hard to follow which class is where. Ben: Fair enough, but I'd still take it over the old one.” Ben = ii (improvement); Priya = iii (confusing); option i is a decoy nobody mentions.
10. Map labelling
Recognise it: a map or floor plan with lettered locations and a list of places to position. What it tests: understanding directions and positions in real time.

Before the audio: orient yourself on the map, find the starting point (“you are here,” the entrance) and trace the paths. During the audio: the speaker takes you on a route; move your finger along the map as they speak. Key position vocabulary: opposite/facing/across from, next to/beside/adjacent to, between/in the middle of, at the end of/at the far end, on your left/right, in the corner, just past/beyond, behind/in front of, turn left/right, go straight on.

Traps: a corrected direction (“go left, sorry, right”); a route described out of order; left/right depending on the direction of travel. Beginner mistake: stops tracking the route and tries to guess from the map alone, or confuses left/right after a turn. Expert approach: physically follows the described route step by step.

Worked example: locate the gift shop. “Come in through the main entrance. The café is immediately on your right. Walk straight past it, and the gift shop is the second door on your left, just before the exit.” You walk the route, passing the café, then count doors on the left to the second one.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: In map tasks, put your pen on the “you are here” point before the audio starts and physically move it as the speaker gives directions. Candidates who track with the pen rarely get lost; candidates who stare at the whole map trying to hold it in their head usually do.
blocks.bn: Map প্রশ্নে অডিও শুরুর আগে কলম you are here পয়েন্টে রাখুন, নির্দেশ অনুযায়ী নড়ান। কলম দিয়ে পথ ধরে গেলে হারিয়ে যান না।

blocks.text: 11. Diagram labelling

Recognise it: a picture of an object, machine, plan, or process, with parts to be labelled. What it tests: matching spoken descriptions of position, function, and shape to parts of an image — common in Part 4 and technical Part 2 talks.

Before the audio: study the diagram and understand how its parts relate; predict the kind of word each label needs. During the audio: the speaker describes the object in a logical order (top to bottom, outside to inside, order of use), locating each part with position and function language.

Traps: unfamiliar technical vocabulary; parts described by function rather than named directly; losing orientation on the diagram. Beginner mistake: freezes on an unfamiliar word and misses the next two labels. Expert approach: uses position and function clues to place a part even when the exact word is new.

Worked example: label the “outlet” on a water filter diagram (inlet top, chamber middle, tap bottom). “Water enters through the inlet at the top, passes down through the filtering chamber in the centre, and finally leaves through the outlet at the very bottom.” Position (“at the very bottom”) and function (“water leaves through”) place the outlet even without knowing the word.
12. Short answer

Recognise it: a direct question answered in a few words within a stated word limit (“What time does the museum close?”). What it tests: catching a specific fact and reporting it concisely — close to completion but framed as a question.

Before the audio: predict the answer's shape from the question word (what, where, how much, who). During the audio: listen for the specific fact and ignore surrounding detail; respect the word limit strictly.

Traps: the same distractors as completion (corrections, two-option choices); a question asking for two things (“Name TWO items”). Beginner mistake: writes a full phrase where the limit allows two words, or answers a related detail rather than the exact question. Expert approach: answers the precise question word and trims to the limit.

Worked example: “What must visitors leave at reception?” (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS) — “Before the tour, everyone needs to hand in any large bags at reception, though small handbags are fine to keep.” Answer: large bags — “small handbags are fine” is a related-information decoy.
Expert thinking: a matching task under load

Part 3, matching three students to research topics (climate, migration, housing). “Tutor: Have you all picked topics? Aisha: I'm doing housing, though I nearly chose migration. Tom: I've gone for migration. Lena: I was going to do housing too, but Aisha took it, so I'll do climate.” A beginner pencils Aisha to migration and Lena to housing by matching the nearest noun — both wrong. An experienced student gets Aisha and Tom right but hesitates on Lena. An expert candidate tracks the verb of choice for each person, not the nearest noun: Aisha “nearly chose” migration but is doing housing; Lena “was going to do housing but” ended on climate. The decoys were the abandoned choices. The lesson repeats across every selection type: match on the decision, never on the nearest word.
Practice
Drill 5.1 (Level 3): Multiple choice

blocks.label: Drill 5.1 (Level 3): Multiple choice
blocks.prompt: Q: “What does the speaker like most about the new office?” A) the location B) the light C) the space. Transcript: “It's bigger than the old one, which is nice, and the commute's easier now. But honestly, what I love is how bright it is, windows on every side.”
blocks.answer: B, the light. Space and location are mild positives (decoys); “what I love is how bright it is” is the verdict, paraphrased by “bright, windows on every side.” Choosing C because “bigger” came first is the classic mention-not-endorsement error.

blocks.text: Drill 5.2 (Level 4): Multiple-answer

blocks.label: Drill 5.2 (Level 4): Multiple-answer (choose TWO)
blocks.prompt: Q: “Which TWO activities are included in the ticket?” A) boat ride B) lunch C) guide D) museum entry E) parking. Transcript: “Your ticket covers the boat ride and a guided tour. Lunch you pay for separately, and there's no museum entry included. Parking's free but that's for everyone, not part of the ticket.”
blocks.answer: A (boat ride) and C (guide) — both affirmed. Lunch and museum entry are explicitly rejected; parking is a related-information decoy (free, but not part of the ticket). Three options were named only to be denied.

blocks.text: Drill 5.3 (Level 4): Matching

blocks.label: Drill 5.3 (Level 4): Matching
blocks.prompt: Match Ravi and Sara to a view (i. too expensive, ii. well organised, iii. too long). Transcript: “Ravi: The conference ran smoothly, everything on time. Sara: True, but three full days was more than I needed. Ravi: I didn't mind the length, honestly.”
blocks.answer: Ravi = ii, well organised (“ran smoothly, everything on time”). Sara = iii, too long (“three full days was more than I needed”). Nobody mentions cost, so i is a decoy. Ravi “didn't mind the length” tempts you to attach length to Ravi, but he holds the organised view. Match on who holds the view.

blocks.text: Drill 5.4 (Level 3): Map labelling

blocks.label: Drill 5.4 (Level 3): Map labelling (describe the position)
blocks.prompt: Locate the “first aid room.” Transcript: “From the reception, head down the main corridor. Pass the toilets on your left, and the first aid room is right at the end, facing you.” Describe where the first aid room is, in map terms.
blocks.answer: At the far end of the main corridor, facing you (opposite the entrance to the corridor), past the toilets which are on the left. Strategy: walk the route from reception rather than reading the map cold; “right at the end, facing you” is the key position phrase.

blocks.text: Drill 5.5 (Level 3): Short answer

blocks.label: Drill 5.5 (Level 3): Short answer
blocks.prompt: Q: “How long is the guarantee?” (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER) Transcript: “The product comes with a one-year guarantee as standard, and you can extend it to three years for a small fee.”
blocks.answer: One year / 1 year. The question asks for the standard guarantee length; “three years” is the two-option distractor (the paid extension), not the standard guarantee. Trim to the limit: “one year,” not the full phrase.

chapters.title: File 06: Special Problems, the Recovery System, and Time Strategy
chapters.summary: Spelling, numbers, dates, addresses, accents, and fast speech; the five-step Recovery System for a missed answer; and how to use the pauses on the computer-delivered test.

blocks.text: The earlier files taught you how to attack questions. This file deals with the things that go wrong in the middle of a real test: the tricky detail you cannot catch, the answer you miss, the moment you lose your place, and the clock. These are the problems that quietly cost good candidates a whole band, and every one has a concrete fix.
PART 9
Special Listening Problems

Spelling is tested directly, because a misspelled answer is a wrong answer. Names and unusual words are very often spelled out letter by letter. Write the letters as fast as you hear them, in rough capitals. Watch the letter pairs that sound alike — B/P, D/T, G/J, V/B, M/N, and the vowels E/I/A — and listen for “double” (two of that letter) and for a confirming second pass.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: Learn the English alphabet by sound until it is automatic, especially the confusable pairs. In the exam you will not have time to think “was that a G or a J?” You must know it instantly.
blocks.bn: ইংরেজি বর্ণমালার উচ্চারণ, বিশেষ করে G/J, B/P, E/I-এর মতো কাছাকাছি শব্দের অক্ষরগুলো ঝটপট চিনতে শিখুন। পরীক্ষায় ভাবার সময় থাকবে না।

blocks.text: Numbers: two problems catch almost everyone. First, the “-teen” vs “-ty” pair (thirteen vs thirty) — “thirTEEN” stresses the end, “THIRty” stresses the front. Second, digit strings: write each digit as you hear it; “double” means two of the next digit, “triple” means three; “nought point five” or “zero point five” is 0.5; do not try to hold a long number in your head and write it at the end.

Dates: a date can need a day, month, year, or all three, and the order can vary (“the third of March” = “March the third”). Years have two common spoken forms (1985 = “nineteen eighty-five”; 2005 = “two thousand and five” or “twenty oh five”). Predict which part you need from the gap, and write years as four digits unless told otherwise.

Addresses usually combine a house/flat number, street name, and often a postcode; unusual street names may be spelled. Expect the number first, then the street, then the postcode, and watch for corrections — house numbers are a favourite spot for the correction trap.

Telephone numbers: “0” is usually “oh” in British English, sometimes “zero”; “double” and “triple” apply as with all numbers. Write digits straight down as a single string, decoding as you go, without worrying about grouping.

Names are anchors, so they are gold, but only if spelled correctly. If a name is spelled, catch the letters; if unspelled and common, trust the standard spelling; if unsure, listen for the confirmation.

Accents: IELTS uses a range of native accents (British, North American, Australian, New Zealand, and more). Do not panic at an unfamiliar accent — the content words carry the meaning, and your prediction and keyword work do not change. Practise with a variety of accents in advance.

Fast speech runs words together and drops weak sounds. Stop trying to catch every word; rely on prediction to tell your ear what to wait for, and listen for the stressed content words, which stay clear even in fast speech.

Unfamiliar vocabulary is normal and rarely fatal. Do not freeze on an unknown word — the context and the gap's predicted shape usually let you catch it anyway; freezing to work it out is how you miss the next two answers.

Losing concentration is inevitable, especially in the long Part 4 monologue. Spend attention on the approach to each answer and relax slightly in the gaps between; if you feel your mind drifting, use the question numbers as concrete anchors to pull focus back.

Losing your place: use anchors. Listen for the next name, number, or signpost and match it to a question on your page; the questions follow the audio order, so one landmark relocates you instantly. Do not try to reconstruct what you missed — just rejoin at the next landmark.
Confusing two speakers is one of the biggest Part 3 errors. Fix each speaker by name and voice at the start, and note “who” as well as “what” as opinions land.

Multiple-choice overload: with long options you can run out of reading time before the audio starts. Read the question stems first, all of them, then read the options for each question only as the audio approaches it — do not try to read every option of every question up front.
PART 10
The Recovery System
The cost of a missed answer is not the answer. It is the answers you miss while chasing it. Protect the future by abandoning the past instantly.

Here is the mechanism that destroys scores: you miss question 5, and instead of moving on, your mind stays on it. While you are looking backwards, the audio delivers the answers to 6 and 7. One miss has become three. This cascade, not the original miss, is what separates a 6 from an 8.

items: 1. RECOGNISE. Notice, calmly, that the answer has gone. No emotion, just a fact.
2. LEAVE. Let it go completely. Put a small mark by the question number and release it.
3. RESET. Bring your attention fully to the present. The past question is closed.
4. FOLLOW. Move your eyes to the next question and rejoin the audio at that landmark.
5. RECOVER. In the final review, return to marked questions and make your best guess. Never leave a blank — a guess can score, a blank cannot.

blocks.text: That is the whole system: recognise, leave, reset, follow, recover. The hard step is LEAVE, because the instinct is to chase. Train yourself to feel the chase starting and drop it on purpose.

blocks.title: Tutor Insider Tip
blocks.text: Practise missing on purpose. In a practice test, when you miss an answer, watch whether your mind chases it, and force the reset. The candidates who score highest are not the ones who never miss; they are the ones whose misses stay contained to a single mark.
blocks.bn: ইচ্ছে করে উত্তর মিস সামালানোর অনুশীলন করুন। মন পেছনে ছুটছে কিনা খেয়াল করে দ্রুত সামনে ফিরুন।

blocks.text: PART 11
Listening Time Strategy

Listening has a fixed rhythm you do not control: the audio plays, the pauses come where they come, and the test ends when it ends. Your strategy is about using the time you are given, especially the pauses, with maximum efficiency.

Each part follows the same shape: a voice tells you to look at questions, a short pause to read, the audio plays and you answer, then you move to the next set. Use every pause to read ahead, and never fall behind the audio. Do not use pauses to admire answers you already have — use them to predict shapes, mark keywords, and understand multiple-choice options for what is coming. If you finish early, read into the next set and bank the time.

On the computer-delivered test there is no ten-minute transfer; you type answers directly and get only about two minutes to review at the end. Capture every answer cleanly the first time. Treat the final two minutes as a focused check, not a rescue: fill any blank with a best guess, check spellings of names and places, confirm singular or plural, and confirm every word limit — in that priority order.

Manage the difficulty curve: Part 1 is easiest, Part 4 hardest. Bank all the cheap Part 1 marks with full care, since they count exactly as much as the hard ones later, then keep your concentration highest going into the dense Part 4.

rows: Blanks — fill every one with a guess
Word limits — trim any answer that runs over
Singular or plural, where the grammar decides it
blocks.caption: Grammar-heavy proofreading is not the priority here, since Listening answers are short. Blanks and word limits win the most marks in the least time.

blocks.text: The perfect Listening routine

items: Before the test: know the format cold, know the alphabet and numbers by sound, and practise on a screen with a range of accents.
At the start of each part: read the questions in the pause, predict every gap's shape, mark one keyword per question, pre-load likely paraphrases.
During the audio: listen for meaning and anchors, catch answers live and write them at once, wait through distractors for the signal, stay one question ahead with your eyes.
When you miss one: recognise, leave, reset, follow. Mark it and move on without chasing.
Between parts: use every pause to read into the next set and bank time.
At the end: in the final two minutes, fill blanks, trim to word limits, fix spellings, confirm singular or plural.

blocks.text: Practice
Drill 6.1 (Level 2): Decode the numbers and letters

blocks.label: Drill 6.1 (Level 2): Decode the numbers and letters
blocks.prompt:
Write what the speaker means.
1. “It's double three, seven, oh, five.”
2. “The reference is B as in Bravo, then triple two.”
3. “She was born in nineteen ninety-eight.”
4. “The cost is nought point seven five.”
5. “That's thirty, three-zero, not thirteen.”
blocks.answer: 1. 33705. 2. B222. 3. 1998. 4. 0.75. 5. 30 — the speaker spells it out and contrasts it with thirteen, exactly the -teen vs -ty trap.

blocks.text: Drill 6.2 (Level 3): Catch the spelling with a correction

blocks.label: Drill 6.2 (Level 3): Catch the spelling with a correction
blocks.prompt:
Write the final answer.
1. “The name's Stefan, S-T-E-F-A-N, no sorry, with a V, S-T-E-V-A-N.”
2. “Post it to 19 Bly Road, that's B-L-Y, actually it's 90 Bly Road.”
blocks.answer:
1. Stevan — the first spelling is the decoy, corrected by “no sorry, with a V.”
2. 90 Bly Road — the street spelling is confirmed and unchanged; the house number is corrected from 19 to 90.

blocks.text: Drill 6.3 (Level 3): Run the recovery process

blocks.label: Drill 6.3 (Level 3): Run the recovery process
blocks.prompt: You are on question 12. You realise you completely missed question 11 while writing 10. The speaker is now clearly giving information for 12. What should you do, step by step?
blocks.answer: RECOGNISE that 11 is lost, calmly. LEAVE it, marking it lightly. RESET to the present. FOLLOW the audio into question 12, catching it live — do not try to reconstruct 11 while 12 is being spoken, or you lose 12 as well. RECOVER 11 with a guess in the final review. Sacrificing 11 to save 12 is the correct trade; trying to save 11 loses both.

blocks.text: Drill 6.4 (Level 2): Fix the place

blocks.label: Drill 6.4 (Level 2): Fix the place
blocks.prompt: You look up and do not know which question the speaker is on. The speaker says “and the final stage is the inspection.” Your questions are a flow-chart of five stages. What do you do?
blocks.answer: Use the landmark to fix your place: “the final stage” plus “inspection” tells you the speaker is on the last box of the five-stage chart. Jump straight to the final gap and catch its answer; recover any missed middle boxes in the final review rather than panicking about them now.
